On October 16, 1966, Wenjack ran away from the school with two friends, Ralph and Jackie MacDonald. They stayed with the MacDonalds' uncle, Charley Kelley, at Redditt, which is 31 km from Kenora. Wenjack decided to go back to Ogoki Post by following railroad tracks. Wenjack walked for 36 hours. He was wearing a windbreaker. The temperature was −6 °C. Bruises on Wenjack's body showed that he fell several times. A CN railway engineer found Wenjack's body on October 23 at 11:20AM and called the Ontario Provincial Police. The coroner determined the cause of death to be hunger and exposure. Wenjack was buried at the reserve on October 27, 1966. The Canadian government started an investigation into Wenjack's death. It concluded the investigation, saying that: Chanie Wenjack is a symbol of how students at these schools stood up to the abuses and suffering they experienced there. A lecture at Trent University was named after Wenjack after Indigenous students asked for a building to be named in his honor. In 2016, a video was made about Wenjack's life. His sister Pearl was featured in it. The Canadian artist Gord Downie released an album with songs about Wenjack. A story on Wenjack's live call the secret path about hs story.
A chanterelle is a mushroom that is used in cooking. It is yellow. A chanterelle looks much like some other mushrooms. About 25% of its dry weight is protein.

Stéphane Charbonnier (; 21 August 1967 – 7 January 2015), better known as Charb, was a French cartoonist, journalist, and caricaturist. He was best known for his work on the satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo. Charb was born in Conflans-Sainte-Honorine. Charb was among the victims who were killed in a shooting at Charlie Hebdo s Paris headquarters on 7 January 2015. He was 47. Stéphane Charbonnier was born in Conflans-Sainte-Honorine on 21 August 1967 and raised in Pontoise.

Charissa Jean Thompson (born May 4, 1982) is an American television host and sportscaster., she works for Fox Sports. Previously, Thompson worked for ESPN, Versus, GSN and the Big Ten Network. She was the co-host of SportsNation with Marcellus Wiley until June 2013. She became the host of Fox Sports Live on the new Fox Sports 1 network on August 17, 2013. She also was one of the hosts of Ultimate Beastmaster. From 2014 to 2017, Thompson was a co-host on the syndicated entertainment news program Extra. Thompson was the host of Rockies All Access and WNBA Weekly and covered sports for the Denver Pioneers. Thompson also hosted The 2007 MLB All-Star Game Red Carpet Parade and The Baseball Report. She also hosted BCS Breakdown, Toughest Cowboy, the BCS Show, and Friday Night Tailgate for FSN as well as a co-host for Big Saturday Night for the Game Show Network as well as Big Ten's Best for the Big Ten Network. She also did reporting for Shaq vs. as well as an ice-level reporter for the NHL on Versus with the lead broadcast team of Mike Emrick and Eddie Olczyk. Thompson hosted NFL Now Updates and Fast Track to Fame. She replaced Michele Breade as co-host of SportsNation with Colin Cowher.

Charlemagne Masséna Péralte (1886 - 1 November 1919) was a leader in Haiti. He stood against the US Invasion of his country in 1915. He led fighters called the Cacos against the US forces in Haiti. The US needed to get more soldiers because Peraite was difficult to stop. Péralte is a hero in Haiti today. He was born in 1886 in the Hinche. He was named François Borgia Charlemagne Peralte, Date of birth on birth certificate: 10 October 1885. His father was General Remi Massena Peralte. Source for correction: 1885–1985, Un Centenaire; Charlemagne Peralte,, Georges Michel. Privately published in Port-au-Prince, 1989. Footnote, p. 19. Cites research of Roger Gaillard concerning birth and baptismal certificates in Premiere Ecrasement du Cacoism, Port-au-Prince:Le Natal, 1981. Also appears in Douglas Henry Daniels's English translation of Michel's book,Charlemagne Peralte and the First American Occupation. Dubuque, Iowa: Kendall/Hunt Publishing CO., 1996. An officer by career, Charlemagne Péralte was a military officer and chief of the city of Léogane when the US Marines invaded Haiti in July 1915. (See United States occupation of Haiti (1915–1934)) He did not surrender to US troops without fighting, He quit his job and went home to Hinche to take care of his family's land. In 1917, he was arrested. He tried and failed to rob a police payroll. He was sent to labor camp for five years. He escaped. He then got other fighters and began battles against US troops. Péralte's fighters were called "Cacos", a historic name of previous heroes. The Cacos were strong fighters. The US had to send more soldiers. The US had to use airplanes. The "Cacos" attacked Port-au-Prince in 1919, but did not win. Peralte and his "Cacos" fought for two years. He began a new a provisional government in the north of Haiti, He was betrayed by one of his officers, Jean-Baptiste Conzé. Conze led a US soldier into the camp of the "Cacos" near Grand-Rivière Du Nord. The US soldier was Herman H. Hanneken and was promoted afterwards.Péralte was shot in the heart at close range. His body was taken, The US troops took a picture of Charlemagne Péralte's body tied to a door. The picture was shown in many parts of the country. The picture looked like the crucifixion and made Peralte a hero and a martyr. His body was removed from its grave in 1935 for a special funeral. The then-President of Haiti, Sténio Vincent attended. The funeral was held in Cap-Haïtien. His grave can still be seen today. A portrait of Charlemagne Péralte can now be seen on Haitian coins. These coins were stamped by the government of Jean-Bertrand Aristide after his 1994 return.

Charles August Lindbergh, Sr. (January 20, 1859 – May 24, 1924), was a United States Congressman for 6th District of Minnesota from 1907 to 1917. Lindbergh was a member of the Republican Party. He was the father of Charles Lindbergh.

Charles-Louis-Étienne Nuitter (24 April 1828 - 23 February 1899) was a French librettist, translator, and librarian. He is best remembered for having written the libretto for the ballet, Coppélia and for having helped translate Richard Wagner's earliest operas into French.

Charles-Augustin de Coulomb (14 June 1736-23 August 1806) was a French physicist, known for his research on the properties of electricity. He also did research on the friction of fluids. Today, the SI unit for electric charge, the coulomb is named after him. He is one of the 72 people to have his name written on the Eiffel Tower in Paris.

Charles A. Reich (May 20, 1928 – June 15, 2019) was an American legal and social scholar. He was a Professor at Yale Law School when he wrote the 1970 paean to the 1960s counterculture and youth movement, The Greening of America. Reich was born in New York City. Reich died on June 15, 2019 in San Francisco, California at the age of 91.

Charles-Henri Sanson (15 February 1739 – 4 July 1806) was the royal executioner of France during the reign of Louis XVI and was also made the high executioner of the French First Republic. He has executed around 3000 people over the course of 40 or more years.

Sir Charles Babbage (26 December 1791 – 18 October 1871) was an English mathematician, analytical philosopher, mechanical engineer and computer scientist. He was the first person to invent the idea of a computer that could be programmed. Unfinished parts of his mechanisms are on display in the London Science Museum. Charles Babbage was born in England, at 44 Crosby Row, Walworth Road, London. Babbage's father, Benjamin Babbage, was a banker in London who owned the Bitton Estate in Teignmouth. His mother was Betsy Plumleigh Babbage. In 1808, the Babbage family moved into the old Rowdens house in East Teignmouth. His Brain is also on display in the Science Museum in London. Babbage worked and wrote on many ideas of science, engineering and mathematics, but he is most famous for two machines he started and never finished. His Difference Engine would have been a much better calculator than any made before then. His Analytical Engine would have been the first real computer. Knowing that there were many errors in the calculation of mathematical tables, Babbage wanted to find a way to calculate them mechanically, removing errors made by humans. Three different factors seem to have influenced him: a dislike of untidiness; his experience working on logarithmic tables and differential calculus; and work on calculating machines already done by Wilhelm Schickard, Blaise Pascal, and Gottfried Leibniz. He first talked about the principles of a calculating engine in a letter to Sir Humphrey Davy in 1822. Babbage's engines were among the first mechanical computers. His engines were not actually completed because he did not have enough money. Babbage realized that a machine could do the work better and more reliably than a human being. Babbage controlled building of some steam-powered machines that more or less did their job; calculations could be mechanized to an extent. Although Babbage's machines were large machines they were organized in a way similar to modern computer architecture. The data and program memory were separated, operation was instruction based, control unit could make conditional jumps and the machine had a separate I/O unit. Ada Lovelace studied how to program them.

Charles Dalrymple Belgrave (1894–1969) was a British citizen. He was an advisor to the rulers of Bahrain from 1926 until 1957. He first was under Shaikh Hamad ibn Isa Al Khalifa. The he was under Shaikh Salman ibn Hamad Al-Khalifa. During the war he was with the Imperial Camel Corps. He spent two years in Siwa Oasis. He got better at his Arabic at the School of Oriental and African Studies in London. He came to Bahrain in March 1926. He stayed there until 1957. The biggest long-term benefit to the country has said to be the making of schools for girls by his wife Marjorie Belgrave.

Corporal Charles Brown (born 1849) received the United States's highest honor for bravery. It is called the Medal of Honor. Corporal Brown was a United States Marine. He was born in New York City. He enlisted in Hong Kong in 1870. The tracking number for his Medal of Honor is number 169. It is dated 8 February 1872. He received the medal for his actions while stationed aboard the USS Colorado. On board the in action against a Korean fort on 11 June 1871. Assisted in capturing the Korean standard in the center of the citadel of the fort.

Charles Pierre Baudelaire (; 9 April 1821 – 31 August 1867) was a French poet, art critic, and translator. He was born and died in Paris. He is also known for translating the stories of the American writer Edgar Allan Poe into French. His translations helped to make Poe famous in France. Baudelaire's most famous book is Les Fleurs du Mal ("The Flowers of Evil"), first published in 1857. It is a collection of poems written in verse. A smaller collection called Les Épaves ("The Wrecks") followed in 1866. After Baudelaire's death, a collection of his poems in prose was also published. It first appeared under the title Petits Poèmes en prose, but today it is usually called Le Spleen de Paris. Baudelaire also wrote important essays about painting, literature, and music. Baudelaire has an important place in the history of modern poetry. He took many ideas and feelings from the Romantic writers who came before him, but he changed them into something new. His work had a major influence on later French poetry. Younger poets such as Verlaine, Mallarmé, and Rimbaud saw him as a master. In a famous letter written in 1871, Rimbaud called him "the first seer, king of poets, a true God". His life was short and difficult, and many parts of his work are closely connected with his personal experience. His father died when he was five years old. His mother later married an army officer, Jacques Aupick. At first the boy got on with his stepfather, but their relationship later became very difficult. As a young man, he received the money left by his father and quickly spent about half of it. A court then placed the rest under the control of a lawyer. He also had a long and troubled relationship with the actress Jeanne Duval. In 1857, a court decided that Les Fleurs du Mal was an offence against public morals. Baudelaire had to pay a fine, and six poems were banned. He later tried to enter the Académie française, but he failed. He moved to Belgium in 1864. In March 1866, a sudden illness paralysed the right side of his body and left him almost unable to speak. Baudelaire helped to create the image of himself as a poète maudit, or "cursed poet". However, his poetry is carefully constructed and shows close control of language and form. The judgment of 1857 was cancelled by the highest French court only in 1949, almost one hundred years later. By that time, Les Fleurs du Mal had become widely studied and had strongly influenced modern poetry. Charles-Pierre Baudelaire was born on 9 April 1821 at 13 rue Hautefeuille in Paris. His parents were very different from each other. His father, Joseph-François Baudelaire, was sixty-one years old when Charles was born. As a young man, he had become a Catholic priest, but he later left the Church. He worked as a private teacher for the two sons of the count of Choiseul-Praslin, a noble family. For his young pupils, he wrote a small Latin schoolbook and illustrated it himself with watercolour pictures. During the Revolution, when the boys' parents were put in prison, he continued to care for the children and tried to help the family. Later, he held several jobs in the offices of the French Senate. He liked the manners and culture of the 18th century. He loved painting and painted as an amateur. Joseph-François already had a son from his first marriage, Claude-Alphonse, born in 1805. In September 1819, he married Caroline Dufaÿs, who had been born in London in 1793. Her father was a French soldier who had left France during the Revolution. He died in 1795 during a failed landing in Brittany by royalist troops, soldiers who were loyal to the king. Her mother brought her back to France in 1800 but died soon after the journey. Caroline was seven years old. She was then brought up by the family of the lawyer Pierre Pérignon. Her husband was thirty-four years older than she was. Baudelaire's father died on 10 February 1827, when Charles was five years old. The boy kept only a soft and uncertain memory of him, but his love of pictures probably came from his father. After his father's death, Charles and his mother spent the end of the summer of 1827 together in a small house at Neuilly, near Paris. They then lived quietly together in the city for several more months. Baudelaire remembered this short time throughout his life as a lost period of happiness. One of his poems, "Je n'ai pas oublié, voisine de la ville...", keeps the image of the "white house, small but quiet". Much later, in a long letter of 6 May 1861, he reminded his mother of that early time. There had been in his childhood, he wrote, "a period of passionate love" for her. She had been "at once an idol and a comrade". This happy period ended on 8 November 1828, when Caroline married Jacques Aupick, an army officer who later had a successful career. Aupick had been born in 1789. His father was an Irish soldier who served in the French army and died from wounds received in battle. His mother was probably English. Aupick lost both parents when he was a small child and was brought up by a judge in the small northern town of Gravelines. He worked hard and slowly rose to higher positions in the army. He became a general and later the head of the École polytechnique, a famous military school in Paris. He later served as French ambassador in Constantinople and Madrid, and finally became a senator. At first, Charles and his stepfather had a good relationship. It became difficult when Charles made it clear that he wanted to become a writer and nothing else. For many years, books described Aupick as a cruel ruler of the family. The scholar Claude Pichois later gave a more balanced picture. Aupick was an honest and hard-working man, but he could not understand a boy with such sensitive feelings. Baudelaire later remembered his mother's second marriage as a painful break in his childhood. It ended the time of what he called "unbroken tenderness". In his mind, the general came to represent a hard society ruled by money, duty, and success. In 1832, the family moved to Lyon, where the army had sent Aupick. Charles was sent to a boarding school. He remembered these years as dark and closed: a black city, fog, and locked doors. In 1836, Aupick was called back to Paris, and Charles entered the famous Lycée Louis-le-Grand, again as a boarder. He was a gifted but uneven student. He did very well in Latin verse. In 1837, he won the second prize for Latin verse in the concours général. This was a national competition between the best pupils in France. He read a great number of books, but his independent behaviour often annoyed his teachers. In April 1839, the school expelled him. Another pupil had passed him a note during a lesson, and Charles swallowed the paper instead of giving it to the teacher. He finished the school year as a day pupil at another Paris school, the Collège Saint-Louis. In August 1839, he passed the baccalauréat, the French final school examination. These eight years in boarding schools felt like years in prison to him. They gave him a strong knowledge of Latin and of the classical writers, and this learning can be seen throughout his work. At the same time, they left him with a deep and lasting feeling of loneliness. After leaving school, Baudelaire registered as a law student, but he rarely attended classes. He told his older brother that he wanted only one thing: to become independent as soon as possible and live by writing. He spent his time with young poets in the Latin Quarter, including Gustave Le Vavasseur and Ernest Prarond. During this period, he had a relationship with a poor woman called Sara who worked as a prostitute. He also caught a venereal disease, an infection passed on during sex. His biographers usually identify it as syphilis, though the exact diagnosis has been questioned. There was no cure at that time. The illness may have harmed his health throughout his life and helped cause his early death. His mother and General Aupick were worried by his free way of life and by his growing debts. In June 1841, they placed him on a ship called the Paquebot des Mers du Sud, which sailed from Bordeaux for Calcutta. The voyage did not reach its planned destination. A violent storm near the Cape of Good Hope badly damaged the ship. It stopped for repairs at Mauritius, then sailed on to the island of Bourbon, now called La Réunion. There Baudelaire refused to travel any further, and the ship left for Calcutta without him. He came home on another ship, the Alcide, and reached France in February 1842. Aupick was angry, but the voyage became very important for Baudelaire's poetry. The sea, ports, tropical smells, bright light, and distant islands appeared again and again in his work. Poems such as "L'Albatros", "Parfum exotique", and "La Chevelure" were partly based on these memories. When Baudelaire returned to Paris, he turned twenty-one on 9 April 1842. A few weeks later, he received the money left by his father. It was about 100,000 francs, a large amount at the time. He rented rooms on the île Saint-Louis, and in 1843 he moved into the beautiful old hôtel Pimodan, now called the hôtel de Lauzun. There he lived as a "dandy", a man who tries to make his clothes, manners, and whole life into a work of art. He bought expensive clothes, old furniture, paintings, and rare books. A group of artists met in the same house to use hashish. The writer Théophile Gautier took part, and he gave the group its name, the "Club des Hachichins". The meetings took place in the apartment of the painter Fernand Boissard. A doctor named Moreau de Tours also took part. He studied mental illness and used the meetings for his medical research. Baudelaire himself came only rarely because hashish did not interest him much. The novelist Balzac attended one meeting. Baudelaire later told the story in Les Paradis artificiels: Balzac examined the drug, smelled it, and handed it back without touching it. At the hôtel Pimodan, Baudelaire probably met Gautier for the first time, but their real friendship began only in the 1850s. His close companions during these years were the poet Théodore de Banville and the writer Champfleury. He also met Nadar, who later became a famous photographer. Around 1842, he met Jeanne Duval, a woman of colour who had played small parts in a Paris theatre. Almost nothing about her life is known for certain, not even her real family name. In 1859, she told a hospital that she had been born in Saint-Domingue, now Haiti. For almost twenty years, she was his lover. They separated and came back together many times. Nadar saw her for the last time in 1870; she was walking with crutches. Several well-known love poems in Les Fleurs du Mal, including "La Chevelure" and "Le Balcon", are connected with her. In only two years, Baudelaire spent about 44,500 francs, almost half of his fortune. His worried mother went to court. On 21 September 1844, the court decided that a lawyer, Narcisse-Désiré Ancelle, would control the money that remained. From that time, the poet received a small yearly allowance: 2,400 francs at first, about 200 francs each month. Baudelaire felt deeply humiliated. He was twenty-three years old but was treated like a child and had to explain how he spent every franc. The decision made his relationship with his mother more bitter and kept him poor for the rest of his life. He lived with debts, moved again and again from one furnished room to another, and wrote endless letters about money. In the spring of 1855, he told his mother that he had been forced to move six times in a single month. Over his whole life, Claude Pichois counted at least thirty different homes in Paris. He often had to write quickly for newspapers simply to earn enough money to live. Over time, however, he and Ancelle slowly began to trust each other. During his years in Belgium, Baudelaire sent the lawyer some of his most honest and personal letters. Baudelaire first became known to the public not as a poet but as an art critic. In May 1845, he published his first work, the Salon de 1845. He signed it "Baudelaire-Dufaÿs", adding his mother's family name to his own. The book was still close to a simple list of paintings, but its judgments were already strong. Baudelaire said that Eugène Delacroix was the best painter in the exhibition. The little book found very few readers, and Baudelaire himself was soon unhappy with it. A few weeks later, on 30 June 1845, Baudelaire tried to kill himself with a knife in a Paris café. In a farewell letter to Ancelle, he wrote: "I am killing myself because I am useless to others, and dangerous to myself." He also wrote, more strangely: "I am killing myself because I believe that I am immortal, and because I hope." In the same letter, he left almost everything he owned to Jeanne Duval. The wound was real, and for several days he could not leave Jeanne's rooms. He then lived for a while with his mother and the general. But he could not accept the rules of their house, and he soon returned to his free and disordered life. The following year, the Salon de 1846 was a much more important work. It was no longer a list but a complete book of ideas about art. It begins with an unusual address, "To the bourgeois", and asks serious questions. What makes a good critic? What is Romantic art? What is colour? The chapter on colour is one of the most original parts of the book. Baudelaire describes nature as a great concert of colours, in which every tone lives in harmony with the others. For him, colour works like music. To support this idea, he quotes a page by the German writer E. T. A. Hoffmann about the hidden links between colours, sounds, and perfumes. The famous poem "Correspondances" later developed the same idea. Baudelaire again said that Delacroix was better than the painters of the Ingres school and the fashionable painters of the time. He strongly attacked Horace Vernet, a painter famous for pictures of military glory. Some readers have understood this attack as an indirect attack on General Aupick. The most important part of the book is its final chapter, "On the Heroism of Modern Life". Here Baudelaire first explained an idea that became central to his thinking about art. Every period of history has its own kind of beauty. The black coats, crowded streets, and ordinary people of the modern city also have their own beauty and heroism. Artists must learn to see them. During the same years, Baudelaire wrote short pieces for newspapers such as Le Corsaire-Satan. In 1847, he published his only short story, La Fanfarlo. Its hero, Samuel Cramer, is an ironic portrait of the young dandy that Baudelaire had once been. He may have first seen the actress Marie Daubrun, "the woman with the green eyes", on a Paris stage in 1847. The first clear signs of a close relationship, however, date only from 1854. She inspired a second group of love poems, including "L'Invitation au voyage" and "Le Poison". Another important woman was Apollonie Sabatier, called "la Présidente", who welcomed painters and writers into her home. Baudelaire had probably first met her during the 1840s in the circle of the hôtel Pimodan, but their special relationship began in the early 1850s. Between December 1852 and May 1854, he sent her seven letters with poems. He wrote them in a disguised hand and did not sign them. Most of these poems, such as "Réversibilité" and "Le Flambeau vivant", show a more spiritual and ideal kind of love. They form the third great group of love poems in Les Fleurs du Mal. He revealed that he was the author only on 18 August 1857, two days before the trial of his book. He asked for her help and listed "the monsters" for her: the president, the judges, and the prosecutor Pinard, marked "fearsome". Their love story ended at the end of that same month, but she remained a loyal friend. In February 1848, the Revolution of 1848 began in Paris, and Baudelaire took part in it. He was seen in the street fighting carrying a gun. According to one witness, he shouted that General Aupick should be shot. His political anger and his anger against his family had become closely connected. With Champfleury and Toubin, he started a small newspaper called Le Salut public, but only two issues appeared. For several weeks, he then worked for another paper, La Tribune nationale. In June 1848, when the workers of Paris rose again, he is said to have fought on their side. In October, he even went to Châteauroux, in central France, to run a small conservative newspaper, but his ideas shocked its staff and owners. The bloody fighting of June and the coup d'état of 2 December 1851, when Louis-Napoléon took power by force, ended his hopes for political change. "The Second of December took all politics out of my body," he wrote to Ancelle in 1852. If he had voted, he joked in the same letter, he could only have voted for himself. After this, his view of life became much darker. From the writer Joseph de Maistre, he took the Christian idea of original sin, the belief that human beings are born with evil already inside them. This became an important part of his thinking. However, the memory of 1848 never completely left his poetry. Old women, rag-pickers, workers, and other poor and broken people of the Paris streets appear again and again in his poems about the city. In 1847, Baudelaire discovered the work of Edgar Allan Poe in French newspapers. The first story he read was "The Black Cat", in a translation by Isabelle Meunier. Poe's work made a very strong impression on him. Years later, he explained this feeling in a letter to the critic Théophile Thoré. He had translated Poe so patiently, he wrote, "because he resembled me". When he first opened one of Poe's books, he had found, "with terror and delight", subjects that he himself had dreamed about. He had even found whole sentences that he had thought, but that Poe had written twenty years before. Baudelaire saw Poe as a brother. They shared the idea that art should be carefully and consciously made, and both were interested in strange and disturbing subjects. Baudelaire also saw a similar fate in Poe's life: a writer destroyed by a society that cared mainly about money. Baudelaire's first translation of Poe, the story "Mesmeric Revelation", appeared in 1848. For the next seventeen years, he gave a large part of his energy to translating Poe and making French readers admire him. He taught himself enough English for this work and questioned Americans who lived in Paris. In 1852, he published his first long essay about Poe's life and work. His translations appeared one after another through the publisher Michel Lévy: Histoires extraordinaires in 1856, Nouvelles Histoires extraordinaires in 1857, Les Aventures d'Arthur Gordon Pym in 1858, Eurêka in November 1863 (the printed date is 1864), and Histoires grotesques et sérieuses in 1865. Even the title Histoires extraordinaires was not Poe's own title. Baudelaire created it for French readers. The first printing of 6,000 copies sold quickly. This work helped Baudelaire in three ways. It gave him his most regular income, more than all his own books together. It also gave him the respectable position of a serious working writer. Finally, translating Poe helped him develop his own art. Poe's ideas about short works and carefully planned effects made Baudelaire even more interested in tight form and careful work. Baudelaire's picture of Poe as a great mind destroyed by a society ruled by money was also a picture of himself. By defending the American writer, Baudelaire was also attacking his own age. The book published in 1857 was the result of about fifteen years of work. As early as 1845, Baudelaire announced a future book called Les Lesbiennes. In 1848 and 1851, he used the title Les Limbes. The final title, Les Fleurs du Mal, perhaps suggested by the writer Hippolyte Babou, appeared in 1855. That year, the respected Revue des deux mondes published eighteen of the poems under this title. This publication introduced the poems to a larger group of readers. These poems later formed the centre of the book. Baudelaire was never satisfied with his work and continued to delay the complete book. In the end, his friend Auguste Poulet-Malassis, a young printer from Alençon, published it. Poulet-Malassis remained loyal to Baudelaire until the end and lost money because of this loyalty. On 27 April 1857, General Aupick died. His widow moved to Honfleur, where she lived in a small house above the sea. Baudelaire called it the "toy house". He later spent several useful periods of work there. On 25 June 1857, Les Fleurs du Mal went on sale. About 1,100 copies were printed for sale. About twenty more, printed on fine Holland paper, went to friends such as Delacroix, Gautier, and the poet's mother. The book contained one hundred poems divided into five sections. Fifty-two of them appeared there for the first time; the others had already been published in reviews. It opens with "Au lecteur", or "To the Reader", a poem placed before the numbered series. Its last line became famous: "Hypocrite lecteur, mon semblable, mon frère !" ("Hypocrite reader, my equal, my brother!"). On 5 July, Gustave Bourdin attacked the book violently in the newspaper Le Figaro. Two days later, the government asked the courts to act. Baudelaire did not give in. On 9 July, he told his mother that the book was clothed in "a cold and sinister beauty" and had been made "with fury and patience". It would live, he wrote, in the memory of educated readers beside the best poems of Hugo, Gautier, and even Byron. In the days that followed, the police began taking copies from Paris shops. On 11 July, Baudelaire sent his publisher a hurried note: "Quick, hide the whole edition, and hide it well." He himself had already hidden fifty copies. The authorities brought the author and his publishers before the sixth court of the Seine. They were accused of offending public and religious morals. The trial took place on 20 August 1857. The prosecutor was Ernest Pinard, the same man who had prosecuted Flaubert's Madame Bovary in January. In that earlier case, Flaubert had been found not guilty. Pinard handled Baudelaire's case carefully. He almost abandoned the religious part of the accusation and concentrated on the poems about the body and sexual desire. Baudelaire's lawyer, Gustave Chaix d'Est-Ange, failed to save the book. The court gave its judgment on the same day. It found no offence against religion, but it found an offence against public morals. Baudelaire had to pay a fine of 300 francs, and each publisher had to pay 100 francs. The court ordered six poems to be removed: "Lesbos", the first poem called "Femmes damnées", "Le Léthé", "À celle qui est trop gaie", "Les Bijoux", and "Les Métamorphoses du vampire". The judges said that the poems showed the body in a coarse and direct way that offended accepted ideas of modesty. The poems were therefore punished not mainly for their ideas, but for the open way in which they represented the body and sexual desire. At that time, "realism" in literature was a major subject of public debate. Baudelaire had hoped that the trial would show the public that he had done nothing wrong, and the judgment affected him deeply. He said again and again that the court had misunderstood the book. In notes prepared for his lawyer, he argued that Les Fleurs du Mal had to be judged as a complete work. When read as a whole, he said, its moral meaning was clear: it showed horror at evil. To describe evil with horror was not the same as praising it. He did not appeal against the judgment. At the end of 1857, he wrote to the Empress, and in January 1858 his fine was reduced to fifty francs. Some writers supported him. Four favourable reviews, by Thierry, Dulamon, Asselineau, and Barbey d'Aurevilly, were printed together in a small booklet for the judges because most newspapers had refused to publish them. Flaubert and Custine sent Baudelaire warm messages, while Sainte-Beuve gave him careful private support. From his island of exile, Victor Hugo wrote that the poems "shine and dazzle like stars". In October 1859, Victor Hugo sent Baudelaire an open letter. Baudelaire had asked for it as a preface to his small book on Gautier. In this letter, Hugo thanked him for two poems dedicated to him and made a famous judgment. Baudelaire, he wrote, had created "a new shiver", or un frisson nouveau, in art. Hugo also politely explained that their ideas about art were different. He himself had never believed in art for art's sake, he wrote, but always in art for progress. The six poems remained banned until 31 May 1949. On that date, under a law passed in 1946, the highest French court cancelled the judgment of 1857. The trial did not stop Baudelaire's work. Instead, it pushed him to give the book a new form. During the following years, he wrote some of his greatest poems, including "Le Voyage", "Le Cygne", "Les Sept Vieillards", and "Les Petites Vieilles". "Le Voyage", the longest poem in the book, was probably written at Honfleur, in his mother's house, at the start of 1859. The last three were dedicated to Victor Hugo. He also prepared a second edition of Les Fleurs du Mal. It was published in the first days of February 1861, and 1,500 copies were printed. The six banned poems were removed, and thirty-two new poems were added. Nearly all of the new poems had already appeared in reviews. Only one, "La Fin de la journée", was printed here for the first time. Baudelaire had wanted a symbolic picture at the front of the book. The engraver Félix Bracquemond could not produce one that satisfied him, so the edition carried an engraved portrait of the poet instead. The new edition also contained a new section called "Tableaux parisiens", or "Paris Pictures". Scholars usually use this 1861 edition today because it was the last one published under Baudelaire's own control. Government lawyers examined it but did not take any action. Other books appeared during the same period. Les Paradis artificiels (1860) is a two-part study of hashish and opium. Its second part is a French version, with Baudelaire's own comments, of Thomas De Quincey's book about opium. In February 1860, after hearing Wagner's music in Paris, Baudelaire sent the composer a letter full of admiration. Richard Wagner et Tannhäuser à Paris (1861) strongly defended the composer after Paris audiences had laughed at his work. In Wagner's music, Baudelaire found support for his own idea of "correspondences", or links between the senses and the arts. He also wrote essays about living writers such as Hugo, Gautier, and Banville. In 1859, he published the Salon de 1859. In this long essay, he defended imagination. He called it "the queen of the faculties". He argued against the idea that art should only copy the real world exactly. Photography, he wrote, should remain only "the servant of the sciences and the arts". In 1863, Le Figaro finally published Le Peintre de la vie moderne, or "The Painter of Modern Life", about the artist Constantin Guys. Guys drew quick scenes of daily life for newspapers. His drawings had given Baudelaire back his pleasure in art after French painting in 1859 had disappointed him. The essay was mostly written by 1860. It became Baudelaire's most important explanation of what "modern" art should be. In December 1861, Baudelaire took a step that surprised his friends. He became a candidate for a seat in the Académie française, first for the seat of Eugène Scribe and then for that of the churchman Lacordaire. His friends were surprised by the decision. It was partly meant to shock people and partly an attempt to appear respectable to his mother. However, Baudelaire was also serious. He believed that the Académie, the most important French literary institution, should respect pure poetry and should also recognise the writer who had been condemned in 1857. Candidates had to visit members of the Académie and ask for their support. These visits did not go well for Baudelaire. Only the old poet Alfred de Vigny welcomed him warmly, and Vigny advised him to withdraw. During the campaign, Sainte-Beuve published an article that praised him but also made fun of him. He called Baudelaire a "nice boy" who had built a "strange kiosk" at the extreme point of "the romantic Kamchatka". Kamchatka is a distant, cold land at the eastern end of Russia. The joke placed Baudelaire at the far edge of literature. Baudelaire withdrew in February 1862. These years of intense work were also years in which his health became worse. From January 1860, Baudelaire suffered his first attacks affecting his brain. In April 1862, his half-brother Alphonse died. His illness was a form of paralysis similar to the one that later struck the poet. Jeanne Duval, partly paralysed since 1859, lived in a care home that he paid for. Poulet-Malassis, deeply in debt, went to prison in 1862 and lost his business. In 1863, he moved to Belgium to escape further legal action. Baudelaire's own money problems also became worse. On 1 November 1863, he sold Michel Lévy the full rights to his five Poe volumes. The price was only 2,000 francs. After this sale, he lost his most regular source of money. In January 1862, Baudelaire noted a strange warning in his private papers. He had felt pass over him "the wind of the wing of imbecility", a failing of the mind. He believed that his death was approaching. During this period, he gave most of his attention to the major work of his last years: the short prose poems. They appeared in groups in newspapers, mainly from 1861 onward. In 1862, La Presse published twenty of them with Baudelaire's opening letter to Arsène Houssaye. His death stopped the collection at fifty poems. On 24 April 1864, Baudelaire arrived in Brussels. He had two hopes. First, he planned to earn money by giving public lectures at the Cercle artistique et littéraire, a private cultural club. Second, he hoped to sign a contract for his complete works with Lacroix and Verboeckhoven, the publishing house that had published Hugo's Les Misérables. The first lecture, about Delacroix, went well and was even praised in the Brussels press. But the next lectures, about Gautier, opium, and hashish, attracted smaller and smaller audiences. There were five lectures in all. Baudelaire had agreed by word of mouth to receive one hundred francs for each one. Instead of five hundred francs, the club sent him only one hundred, with a letter of apology. Lacroix and Verboeckhoven were invited to every lecture but never came. Baudelaire had planned to remain for two months, but he stayed for two years at the hôtel du Grand-Miroir. During this time, he was poor, disappointed, and increasingly bitter. He then began a new writing project: a violent book against Belgium. He collected notes under several changing titles, including Pauvre Belgique !, but he never completed the work. He also wrote a group of sharp satirical poems called the Amoenitates Belgicae. Scholars have argued that his hatred was directed at more than Belgium. Its real target may have been the whole modern world of money and business, as well as Baudelaire's anger at his own failure. He himself said that the Belgian book would be only the first step towards another work called Pauvre France !. The Belgian years also produced Les Épaves in 1866, a small book of twenty-three poems secretly printed in Brussels by Poulet-Malassis. Only 260 copies were made, with the false address "Amsterdam" on the title page. The artist Félicien Rops drew a strange picture for the front. The book included the six banned poems, so the copies meant for France had to cross the border in secret. In May 1868, after the poet's death, a court in Lille even ordered the destruction of Les Épaves. Baudelaire's health was now very poor. Around 15 March 1866, he visited the church of Saint-Loup in Namur with Poulet-Malassis and Félicien Rops. While he was looking at the carved confessionals, he suddenly felt dizzy and fell on the stone floor. He claimed that his foot had slipped, and his friends pretended to believe him. During the following days, his condition became worse. By the end of March, the right side of his body was paralysed, and he had lost the power of speech. He could say almost nothing except a short curse, "crénom". However, part of his mind remained clear, and he recognised the friends who came to visit him. At first, he was cared for in a religious hospital in Brussels. His mother travelled quickly from Honfleur to be with him. In July 1866, Baudelaire was brought back to Paris and placed in a care home in the rue du Dôme. There Mme Paul Meurice played Wagner's music for him on the piano. He remained in this condition for more than a year. Baudelaire died quietly on the morning of 31 August 1867, at the age of forty-six, with his mother at his side. On that same day, a Paris review, the Revue nationale et étrangère, printed one of his last prose poems. On 2 September, he was buried in Montparnasse Cemetery in the same grave as General Aupick. About one hundred people came to the church of Saint-Honoré d'Eylau, and fewer still walked to the grave because many Parisians were away for the summer. Banville and Asselineau spoke there. Among those present were the painter Manet and the young poet Verlaine. His mother died in 1871 and was buried in the same grave. In 1902, a large memorial designed by José de Charmoy was built in the same cemetery. After Baudelaire's death, his writings were collected and arranged. The rights to all his works were sold at auction on 4 December 1867. His friend Asselineau bought them for the publisher Michel Lévy for only 1,750 francs. Between 1868 and 1870, Lévy published the Œuvres complètes, or "Complete Works", in seven volumes, edited by Asselineau and Banville. Three of the seven volumes contained the Poe translations. A third edition of Les Fleurs du Mal, published in 1868 with a preface by Gautier, included new poems, but scholars no longer follow its order. Two volumes, Curiosités esthétiques and L'Art romantique, collected his essays about art and literature. The Petits Poèmes en prose appeared in 1869. His private notebooks, including Fusées and Mon cœur mis à nu, his writings about Belgium, and his letters appeared slowly over many years. Editors continued this work from Eugène Crépet's edition of 1887 to the major scholarly editions of the 20th century. Yves-Gérard Le Dantec prepared the first Pléiade edition of the complete works. Claude Pichois revised it in 1961 and later replaced it with his own two-volume edition of 1975 and 1976. Baudelaire always said that his book was a construction, not a simple collection. "The only praise I ask for this book is that people see that it is not a mere album, and that it has a beginning and an end," he wrote to Vigny in 1861. All the new poems of 1861, he added in the same letter, had been made to fit into this chosen frame. Many critics read the order of the poems as a journey of the soul. The 1861 edition has one hundred and twenty-six poems in six sections. Between the two editions, Baudelaire also moved the wine poems to an earlier place, so that each stage prepares the next. "Spleen et Idéal" ("Spleen and the Ideal") is by far the longest, and it lays the base of everything. Man is pulled in two directions: upward, toward beauty and the love of the spirit; downward, toward "spleen", empty time and death. The section moves through the condition of the poet, the theory of beauty and the three love cycles. Then it falls into spleen, marked by four poems that all carry that name. The "Tableaux parisiens", new in 1861, take the drama into the modern city. Here are the crowds, the old men and women, the poor, and the ghosts of a Paris torn up by Haussmann's building works. "Le Vin" ("Wine") and the section called "Fleurs du Mal" (without "Les": that is the name Baudelaire gave it) pass through the false ways out: drink and forbidden pleasure. "Révolte" ("Revolt") pushes the war with religion as far as a prayer to Satan. "La Mort" ("Death") opens onto the last voyage. The book ends with the last line of "Le Voyage": "Au fond de l'Inconnu pour trouver du nouveau !" ("to the bottom of the Unknown to find something new"). The Italian scholar Mario Richter notes that this last poem no longer says "I" but "we". For him, the final departure toward the unknown is a journey made together. Barbey d'Aurevilly had already pointed this out in 1857, when he spoke of a "secret architecture". Baudelaire himself teased his readers about it. In a draft preface, he played with the idea of explaining "why and how I made this book". Such a study, he wrote, might amuse minds in love with "deep rhetoric", the deeper way in which a book is built. But he refused: an artist does not show the public the machinery of his tricks. In 2001, Mario Richter went looking for this deep rhetoric. His two volumes give the first complete reading of the 1861 book. He follows the poems one by one, in order, like a single story. He notes, for example, that the poem numbers run on across the borders of the sections. He also shows that many key words in the book keep two meanings at the same time. For him, this planned double sense is the deep rhetoric itself. It is also why the poems must be read slowly and in order. In Richter's reading, this structure makes the book a kind of drama of human life. The opening address gives its religious frame. Man is a fallen being, in the hands of the Devil. His worst vice is not crime or lust but Ennui: boredom, a soft monster that dreams of scaffolds while smoking its water pipe. The "Mal" of the title has more than one meaning. It is the deep evil in human nature, the evil men do, and the pain and misery of the poor man's life. The poet's task is to change this dark material into something else. A famous line from a draft epilogue for the 1861 edition says it: "You gave me your mud and I turned it into gold." Spleen is one of the central ideas of the book. In Baudelaire the English word means far more than sadness. It is a deep sadness, boredom and disgust with life, felt almost in the body. It joins a deep fear and the painful feeling that time cannot be escaped. The four "Spleen" poems have given the language some of its most famous pictures. The low, heavy sky presses down like a lid. The falling rain looks like the bars of a huge prison. Anguish plants its black flag in the bowed head. On the other side, the "Ideal" is not a safe religious answer. It is a reaching out with no certain end. Beauty, art, perfumes, music and love give short, bright signs of it. The contrast between spleen and the ideal runs through much of the book. The short poem "Correspondances" became a key text for the poets who came after. Nature in it is a temple where man walks through "forests of symbols". Smells, colors and sounds answer one another, so that a smell can be "green" or a sound "sweet". Behind this stand two ideas. The things of the senses are signs of a higher spiritual world: an old religious idea, taken from the thinker Swedenborg. And the different senses open into one another. From this poem comes the picture of the poet as a reader of signs. In an essay of 1861 on Victor Hugo, Baudelaire himself defined the poet as "a translator, a decoder" of these signs. This idea of the poet as a translator is important in Baudelaire's work. Later poets, such as Rimbaud and Mallarmé, took up this idea. Women and love fill almost a third of the book. They are pulled between two poles: worship and hatred, spirit and cruelty. The Jeanne Duval cycle is dark, warm and sometimes bitter. The Sabatier cycle turns the loved one into a being of light. The Marie Daubrun cycle is soft like autumn, with its invitation to a voyage to a country that looks like the loved woman.

Charles Brenton Huggins (September 22, 1901 – January 12, 1997) was a Canadian-born American physician, physiologist, and cancer researcher at the University of Chicago specializing in prostate cancer. He was awarded the 1966 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering that hormones could be used to control the spread of some cancers. Huggins was born on September 22, 1901 in Halifax, Nova Scotia. He studied at Acadia University and at Harvard University. Huggins died on January 22, 1997 in Chicago, Illinois from natural causes, aged 95.

Henry Charles Bukowski (born Heinrich Karl Bukowski; August 16, 1920 – March 9, 1994) was a German-American poet, novelist, and short story writer. His writing was influenced by the social, cultural, and economic ambience of his home city of Los Angeles. His work addresses the ordinary lives of poor Americans, the act of writing, alcohol, relationships with women, and the drudgery of work. He died of leukemia.

Charles William "Charlie" Bachman III (December 11, 1924 – July 13, 2017) was an American computer scientist. He spent his entire career as an industrial researcher, developer, and manager rather than in academia. He is particularly known for his work in the early development of database management systems. The Bachman diagrams are named after him. He won the Turing Award in 1973. Bachman died on July 13, 2017 at his home in Lexington, Massachusetts of Parkinson's disease at the age of 92.

Charles Henry Branscomb (June 16, 1822 January 3, 1891) was a person in the New England Emigrant Aid Society. He and Charles L. Robinson helped create the city of Lawrence, Kansas in 1854. Branscomb was born in Newmarket, New Hampshire on June 16, 1822. He graduated from Dartmouth College in 1845, and he graduated from Cambridge in 1848. In the 1850s, he joined the New England Emigrant Aid Company. In 1854, he and Charles Robinson went to the Kansas Territory. They were looking for a good place to make a city. They found a place, and it became Lawrence, Kansas. He led the first people to Lawrence. In the 1860s, Branscomb moved to St. Louis. In 1874, he came back to Lawrence. He ran for Governor of Kansas, but he lost. In 1890, he moved to Denver, Colorado. He died on January 3, 1891 of pneumonia.

Charles Bernstein (born April 4, 1950) is an American poet, essayist, editor, and literary scholar. Bernstein is the Donald T. Regan Chair in the Department of English at the University of Pennsylvania. He is one of the most famous members of the Language poets (or L=A=N=G=U=A=G=E poets). In 2006 he was elected a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Bernstein's selected poetry from the past thirty years, All the Whiskey in Heaven, was published in 2010. L E G E N D, with Bruce Andrews, Steve McCaffery, Ron Silliman, Ray DiPalma (1980) The Nude Formalism, with Susan Bee (1989)

Charles Boycott (12 March 1832 – 19 June 1897) was the man after whom the modern word "boycott" was coined. The term is an eponym derived from his surname. He was the first person to be boycotted: farmers in County Mayo, Ireland, started a movement to refuse any trade or social relations with him.

Charles Brook (philanthropist) (1814–1872), English businessman and philanthropist Charles Wortham Brook (1901–1983), London GP and member of the London County Council Charles Brook, a fictional character in the horror web series The Walten Files.

Charles Robert Darwin (12 February 1809 – 19 April 1882) was an English naturalist. He is famous for his work on the theory of evolution. Darwin's book On the Origin of Species was published in 1859. In this book, he put forward much evidence that evolution had occurred. He also proposed natural selection as the way evolution had taken place. Darwin did not know about genetics: he never read the work of Gregor Mendel. Nevertheless, Darwin's explanation of evolution was fundamentally correct. In contrast to Lamarck, Darwin's idea was that the giraffe's neck became longer because those with longer necks survived better. These survivors passed their genes on, and in time the whole species got longer necks. Darwin was born in Shrewsbury, Shropshire. His grandfather, Erasmus Darwin, opposed the slave trade; his father was a doctor. He studied at the University of Edinburgh Medical School and at Christ's College, Cambridge. Despite studying medicine at the University of Edinburgh Medical School, a very influential medical school, Darwin dropped out because he hated the sight of blood and was bored of the lectures there. At Cambridge, he created the Gourmet Club, also known as the Glutton Club, where he would eat exotic animals. In 1843 Darwin, who already had ten children with his wife Emma, bought Down House in the village of Downe, Kent. He lived there for the rest of his life, and today the house and contents are open to the public. In 1882, he was diagnosed with angina pectoris, which then meant coronary thrombosis. He died at Down House from heart failure caused by coronary thrombosis on 19 April 1882 at the age of 73. His last words were to his family, telling Emma, "I am not the least afraid of deathRemember what a good wife you have been to meTell all my children to remember how good they have been to me". While he rested, he repeatedly told Henrietta and Francis, "It's almost worthwhile to be sick to be nursed by you". Darwin spent almost five years on board a Royal Navy exploring ship, the HMS Beagle. He was the guest naturalist, which meant that he was responsible for making collections and notes about the animals, plants, and the geology of the countries they visited. The ship's crew made charts of all the coastal areas, which could be used by the navy wherever it went in the world. At the time, Britain had by far the largest navy in the world, and an empire which was global. Darwin collected everywhere the ship landed. He found huge fossils of recently extinct mammals, experienced an earthquake in Chile, and noticed the land had been raised. He knew of raised beaches elsewhere, high in the Andes, with fossil seashells and trees which had once grown on a sandy beach. Obviously the Earth was constantly changing, with land rising in some places, and sinking in others. He collected birds and insects, and sent shipments back to Cambridge for experts to identify. Darwin was the first dedicated naturalist to visit the Galapagos Islands, off the west coast of Ecuador. He noticed that some of the birds were like mockingbirds on the mainland, but different enough to be placed in separate species. He began to wonder how so many new species came to be on these islands. When Darwin got back to England, he edited a series of scientific reviews of the voyage, and wrote a personal journal which we know as The Voyage of the Beagle. It is one of the great natural history travel diaries. While on the H.M.S. Beagle, and later back home in London, Darwin had come across the ideas of the Rev. T.R. Malthus. Malthus had realised that, although humans could double their population every 25 years, it did not happen in practice. He thought the reason was that a struggle for existence (or resources) limited their numbers. If numbers increased, then famine, wars and diseases caused more deaths. Darwin, who knew that all living things could, in principle, increase their numbers, began to think about why some survived, while others did not.p264-268 His answer took years to develop. The theory of evolution says that all living things on Earth, including plants, animals and microbes, come from a common ancestor by slowly changing throughout the generations. Darwin suggested that the way living things changed over time is through natural selection. This is the better survival and reproduction of those that best fit their environment. Fitting into the place where you live is called adapting. Those who fit best into the place where they live, the best adapted, have the best chance to survive and breed. Those who are less well-adapted tend not to survive. If they do not survive well enough to raise young, this means they do not pass on their genes. In this way, the species gradually changes. The first chapter of the Origin deals with domesticated animals, such as cattle and dogs. Darwin reminded readers of the huge changes mankind had made in its domestic animals, which were once wild species. The changes were brought about by selective breeding – choosing animals with desirable characters to breed from. This had been done generation after generation, until our modern breeds were produced. Perhaps what man had done deliberately, might happen in nature, where some would leave more offspring than others. Darwin noticed that although young plants or animals are very similar to their parents, no two are exactly the same and there is always a range of shape, size, color, and so on. Some of these differences the plant or animal may have got from their own ancestors, but some are new and caused by mutations. When such differences made an organism more able to live in the wild, it would have a better chance to survive, and would pass on its genes to its offspring, and they to their offspring. Any difference that would cause the plant or animal to have less of a chance to live would be less likely to be passed on, and would eventually die out altogether. In this way groups of similar plants or animals (called species) slowly change in shape and form so that they can live more successfully and have more offspring who will survive them. So, natural selection had similarities to selective breeding, except that it would happen by itself, over a much longer time. He first started thinking about this in 1838, but it took a full twenty years before his ideas became public. By 1844 he was able to write a draft of the main ideas in his notebook. Historians think that he did not talk about his theory because he was afraid of public criticism. He knew his theory, which did not discuss religion, raised questions about the literal truth of the Book of Genesis. Whatever the reason, he did not publish his theory in a book until 1859. In 1858 he heard that another biologist, Alfred Russel Wallace, had the same ideas about natural selection. Darwin and Wallace's ideas were first published in the Journal of the Linnaean Society in London, 1858. Then, Darwin published his book the next year. The name of the book was On the Origin of Species by means of Natural Selection, or the preservation of favored races in the struggle for life. This is usually called The Origin of Species. Darwin wrote a number of other books, most of which are also very important. 1838-43: Zoology of the voyage of H.M.S. Beagle: published between 1839 and 1843 in five Parts (and nineteen numbers) by various authors, edited and superintended by Charles Darwin, who contributed sections to two of the Parts: 1838: Part 1 No. 1 Fossil Mammalia, by Richard Owen (Preface and Geological introduction by Darwin) 1838: Part 2 No. 1 Mammalia, by George Robert Waterhouse (Geographical introduction and A notice of their habits and ranges by Darwin) 1839: Journal and remarks (The Voyage of the Beagle) 1842: The structure and distribution of Coral Reefs 1844: Geological observations of volcanic islands 1846: Geological observations on South America 1849: Geology from A manual of scientific enquiry; prepared for the use of Her Majesty's Navy: and adapted for travelers in general. ed. John Herschel. 1851: A Monograph of the Sub-class Cirripedia, with figures of all the species. The Lepadidae; or, Pedunculated Cirripedes. Living barnacles. 1854: A Monograph of the Sub-class Cirripedia, with figures of all the species. The Balanidae (or Sessile Cirripedes); the Verrucidae, etc. 1851: A Monograph on the Fossil Lepadidae, or, Pedunculated Cirripedes of Great Britain. Fossil barnacles. 1854: A Monograph on the Fossil Balanidæ and Verrucidæ of Great Britain 1859: On the Origin of Species by means of natural selection, or the preservation of favoured races in the struggle for life 1862: On the various contrivances by which British and foreign Orchids are fertilised by insects (Fertilisation of orchids) 1865: On the movements and habits of climbing plants (Linnean Society paper, published in book form in 1875) 1868: The variation of animals and plants under domestication 1871: The Descent of Man, and selection in relation to sex 1872: The expression of emotions in Man and animals 1876: The effects of cross and self fertilisation in the vegetable kingdom 1877: The different forms of flowers on plants of the same species 1881: The formation of vegetable mould through the action of worms. The original manuscript books of the Origin of Species were returned to Cambridge University library in 2020. They were stolen 22 years before. A full list of all the books in his library is now available. The roughly 7,400 titles have been listed by John van Wylie at the National University of Singapore.

Charles Dickens (7 February 1812 – 9 June 1870) was an English writer and a social critic who is regarded as one of the great English writers of the 19th century. Charles Dickens was born in Portsmouth, England. His parents were John Dickens (1785-1851), a naval pay clerk, and Elizabeth Barrow (1789–1863). When Dickens was born, he had dyslexia and so he could not read or write properly, unlike other kids. When Charles was 12 years old, his family moved to Camden, London. He worked in a blacking (shoe polish) factory there while his father was in prison for debt. Dickens's hard times in the factory served as a foundation of ideas for many of his novels. Many of them, like Oliver Twist, later became famous. When his great-grandmother died and transmitted money, Charles' father paid off his debts and was released from prison. Charles did not like working and wished to stop after his father had been released. However, his mother said that the family needed the money and so Charles was forced to continue working. Charles then finished his schooling and got a job as an office boy for an attorney. After finding that job dull, he taught himself shorthand and became a journalist who reported on the government. Dickens was a Unitarian. His first book was Sketches by Boz in 1836, a collection of the short pieces that he had been writing for the Monthly Magazine and the Evening Chronicle. This was followed by The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club in 1837. Both books became popular as soon as they were printed. The high production costs of making A Christmas Carol led to reduced profits, and the first edition brought him only rather than the he expected. A year later, the profits were only, and Dickens was deeply disappointed. Charles Dickens died of a stroke on June 9, 1870. He was buried in Poets' Corner in Westminster Abbey. He died 5 years and 3 days after getting into a horrible train accident that killed 10 people and injured another 49. Charles Dickens wrote many books, including: The Mystery of Edwin Drood (1869—1870) (unfinished)

Charles Waddell Chesnutt (June 20, 1858 – November 15, 1932) was an African-American writer. He wrote several books like The Marrow of Tradition and The House Behind the Cedars as well as for a short story about a haunted yard called The Goophered Grapevine. The Conjure Woman, and Other Conjure Tales (1899) The Wife of His Youth, and Other Stories of the Color Line (1899) Mandy Oxendine (written in the 1890s; first published in 1997) Paul Marchand, F.M.C. (written in 1921; first published 1998, University Press of Mississippi) A Business Career (written in the 1890s; first published 2005, University Press of Mississippi) Evelyn's Husband (first published 2005, University Press of Mississippi)

Sir Charles Trevelyan, 1st Baronet (2 April 1807 – 19 June 1886) was a British civil servant, cabinet member, colonial administrator, and oriental scholar best known for his administration of the famine relief effort in Ireland during the Potato Famine, while he was assistant secretary to Her Majesty's Treasury. He has been criticized for not doing enough to help the Irish during the Potato Famine. He wrote a book about the famine called The Irish Crisis.

Charles Correa (1 September 1930 – 16 June 2015) was an Indian architect, urban planner and activist. He is known for the creation of modern architecture in post-Independence India. He was awarded the Padma Shri in 1972, and second highest civilian honour, the Padma Vibhushan in 2006, given by Government of India. He was also awarded the 1984 Royal Gold Medal for architecture, by the Royal Institute of British Architects. Correa died at his home in Mumbai after a brief illness at the age of 84.

Charles Duncan Michener (September 22, 1918 – November 1, 2015) was an American entomologist. He was born in Pasadena, California. He was a leading expert on bees, his magnum opus being The Bees of the World.

Charles E. Merrill Jr. (1920 – November 29, 2017) was an American educator, author, and philanthropist. He was best known for supporting historically black colleges and founding the Commonwealth School in Boston. Merrill Jr. died on November 29, 2017, in Nowy Sącz, Poland at the age of 97.

Charles E. Curran (born March 30, 1934) is an American Roman Catholic priest and moral theologian. He was born in Rochester, New York. He serves at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Texas, as the Elizabeth Scurlock University Professor of Human Values.

Charles Francis "Chuck" Dolan (October 16, 1926 – December 28, 2024) was an American billionaire. He was the founder of Cablevision. Dolan's business controls AMC Networks, MSG Networks, and The Madison Square Garden Company, which at one point were all part of Cablevision itself. Dolan died on December 28, 2024, at the age of 98.

Charles George Reinier Corver (16 January 1936 – 10 November 2020) was a Dutch football referee. He refereed the 1982 World Cup semifinal between Germany and France in Seville, Spain. Corver was referee at two World Cups and two European championships. He refereed four European Cup finals, ten semifinals and a final World Cup for clubs in Argentina. He retired in 1983. Corver was born in Leiden and died in Leidschendam at the age of 84.

Charles Darrow (10 August 1889 — 28 August 1967) was one of the creators/ developers of Monopoly. In the 1930s, Charles met Lizzie Maggie, creator of The Landlord’s Game. They played The Landlord’s Game. Later, Charles Darrow made innovations to the game and developed it into Monopoly. In 1935, he sold Monopoly to Parker Brothers. Darrow died on 28 August 1967, in Bucks County, Pennsylvania at the age of 78.

Charles deWolf "Charlie" Gibson (born March 9, 1943) is a United States former broadcast television anchor and journalist. He was born in Evanston, Illinois. He grew up in Washington, D.C. He was a host of Good Morning America from 1987 to 1998, and 1999 to 2006. He was the anchor of World News with Charles Gibson from 2006 to 2009. In 2008 he was a moderator for the US presidential debates. He graduated in 1965 with a degree in history from Princeton University.
Charles Grandison Finney (August 29, 1792 – August 16, 1875) was a proponent of the Second Great Awakening. He preached several Gospels across the western part of the US.

Charles Fletcher Lummis (March 1, 1859, in Lynn, Massachusetts – November 25, 1928, in Los Angeles, California) was a United States journalist, and an activist for Indian rights and historic preservation.

Charles Matthew "Chuck" Geschke (September 11, 1939 – April 16, 2021) was an American businessman and computer scientist. He was best known for founding the graphics and publishing software company Adobe Inc. with John Warnock in 1982, and co-creating the PDF document format.

Charles Fredrick Wiesenthal (1726–1789) was a German physician and inventor born in 1726. He was awarded the patent for the first known mechanical device for sewing in 1755. One might argue that he invented the sewing machine. He died in 1789.

Charles Grey, 1st Earl Grey, later Baron Grey De Howick (1730-1795) was a British fighter. He fought in the American Revolutionary War. Grey was born into an important family. He was born at their large house in Howick, Northumberland, England. Grey's father was a baronet. They had lived in and ruled Howick since the 1200s. Grey's two older brothers died before they could have their own children, but when Grey was a boy, he did not think he would inherit his father's land. So he went into the military in 1944. Grey fought in the War of Austrian Succession, Jacobite Rebellion, and Seven Years' War. He made friends with other British fighters, for example James Wolfe, William Petty, and the Earl of Shelburne. He was aide-de-camp to Prince Ferdinand of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Grey learned to fight. Grey became lieutenant colonel in 1777. He commanded one of General William Howe's brigades. Grey fought in the Battle of Brandywine and surprised General Anthony Wayne at the Battle of Paoli. At Paoli, Grey told his men to charge with their bayonets. Military historians say it was one of the best moves of the entire war. He told his men to take the flints out of their guns so that they would not make sparks that the Continental soldiers could see or fire accidental gunshots that the Continental soldiers could hear. This got him the nickname "'No Flint' Grey." But some people on both sides of the war said Grey had not acted honorably. They called the Battle of Paoli the "Paoli Massacre" instead. Grey fought at the Battle of Germantown and Battle of Monmouth. He surprised more Continental troops in Tappan, New York and killed them. Later, people would call this the Baylor Massacre. In 1778, King George III promoted Grey to Lieutenant General and made him a knight of the Order of the Bath. Grey retired from the army but only for a short while. He went to Howick and built a new house there, Howick Hall. He hired an architect called William Newton. Then Grey worked as an army administrator. He was aide-de-camp to King George III and fought against the French in Belgium and the Caribbean. King George made Grey governor of Guernsey in 1797. He made Grey a baron in 1801. In 1806, he made Grey 1st Earl Grey and Viscount Howick. Grey married Elizabeth Grey of Southwick in 1762. They had eight children including Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey.

Marc Gabriel Charles Gleyre (2 May 1806 – 5 May 1874) was a Swiss-born painter who spent most of his life working in France, where he became a respected academic artist and an influential teacher. Gleyre was born in Chevilly, near Lausanne, Switzerland. Orphaned around age nine, he was raised by an uncle in Lyon, who sent him to the city’s industrial school. He later studied art under Jean-Claude Bonnefond, then moved to Paris to train at the École des Beaux-Arts under Louis Hersent, and also attended the Académie Suisse, where he learned watercolor techniques from Richard Parkes Bonington. In 1834, Gleyre was selected by American traveler John Lowell Jr. to accompany him through Greece, Turkey, and Egypt, documenting scenes and ethnographic subjects. The journey lasted until 1835, after which Gleyre continued traveling through Egypt and Syria alone. He returned to France in 1838 in poor health, suffering from eye inflammation and fever contracted during the trip. After recovering, Gleyre established a studio in Paris and began producing works that blended classical themes with romantic sentiment. His breakthrough came with “Apocalyptic Vision of St. John” (Salon of 1840). In 1843, his painting “Evening”—later known as “Lost Illusions”—won a second‑class medal and became widely popular.He produced more than 683 works, including La Danse des bacchantes (1849), Sappho (1867), and the unfinished Earthly Paradise. In 1843, Gleyre took over the Paris studio of Paul Delaroche, which became a major training ground for future artists. He charged no tuition, asking only for shared studio expenses. Among his students were several future Impressionist masters, including: His teaching style was known for giving students considerable freedom, encouraging experimentation and plein‑air painting. Gleyre’s work is often associated with classical academic painting, yet he also produced Orientalist works inspired by his travels. His paintings are characterized by allegorical themes, meticulous technique, and contemplative mood. Gleyre closed his studio in 1864 due to an eye ailment. He never married and largely avoided public exhibitions in his later years. He died in Paris on 5 May 1874, three days after his 68th birthday.

François Marie Charles Fourier (;; 7 April 1772 – 10 October 1837) was a French philosopher. He was an important philosopher as an early socialist thinker. He was one of the founders of utopian socialism. Some of his views were seen as radical at the time. Fourier is said to have helped create the word feminism in 1837.
Charles Higounet (13 January 1911 – 8 April 1988) was a French historian and medievalist. He specialised in bastides and the Middle Ages in the southwest of France.

Charles Boardman Hawes (January 24, 1889 – July 16, 1923) was an American writer. He wrote stories about the sea. Some of the stories were true and some were not true. His best-known stories are not true; they are fictional. He died when he was 34 years old. He was the third person who won the Newbery Medal, and he was the first winner who was born in the United States. Hendrik Willem van Loon was born in the Netherlands and Hugh Lofting was born in England. The New York Times said his books were like books written by Robert Louis Stevenson, Richard Henry Dana, Jr., and Herman Melville. Charles Boardman Hawes was born in Clifton Springs, New York. His father was named Charles T. Hawes. Charles Boardman Hawes grew up in Bangor, Maine. In 1911 he graduated from Bowdoin College. He was the editor of the student newspaper there. He studied at Harvard for one year. He worked for a magazine called The Youth's Companion until 1920. He was an editor for another magazine called The Open Road for Boys until he died in 1923. On June 1, 1916, Charles Boardman Hawes married Dorothea Cable. She lived in Northampton, Massachusetts. Her father was George W. Cable, who wrote books. Her mother was Louise S. Bartlett. Charles Boardman Hawes had his first story book published in 1920. It was called The Mutineers: a tale of old days at sea and of adventures in the Far East as Benjamin Lathrop set it down some sixty years ago. He had his second story book published in 1921. It was called The Great Quest: A romance of 1826, wherein are recorded the experiences of Josiah Woods of Topham, and of those others with whom he sailed for Cuba and the Gulf of Guinea. That book was a Newbery Medal Honor Book in 1922. Honor Book means that it did not win but the judges thought that it was a good book anyway. Charles Boardman Hawes wrote two more books before he died. One was called Gloucester, by Land and Sea. It was a true story about Gloucester, Massachusetts, which was the town where Hawes lived. This book was published two days after he died. The other book was called The Dark Frigate, Wherein is told the story of Philip Marsham who lived in the time of King Charles and was bred a sailor but came home to England after many hazards by sea and land and fought for the King at Newbury and lost a great inheritance and departed for Barbados by the same ship, by curious chance, in which he had long before adventured with the pirates. That book won the Newbery Medal for 1924. In 1962 The Dark Frigate also won the Lewis Carroll Shelf Award. After Charles Boardman Hawes died, his publishers held a contest. A $2,000 prize was given to the best book that was like the book which Hawes wrote. The book that won was called The Scarlet Cockerel. It was written by a farm worker named Clifford MacClellan Sublette. Hawes's publishers printed The Scarlet Cockerel in 1925. They also printed two other books that they had gotten from the contest.
